newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Senate steps towards poll with vote.
newsitem.headline: Australian Senate steps towards poll with vote.

text.p: The Australian upper house, the Senate, on Friday imposed what the government called an unacceptable amendment on a bill identified as a potential early-election trigger.

But the social security bill cannot give Prime Minister John Howard the right to dissolve parliament and call an early election unless the government calls the Senate's bluff, presents the bill again at least three months from now and sees it rejected again.
Non-government parties combined in the Senate to amend the bill, under which some young people will be made to work for welfare, to terminate the scheme after a two-year trial.
"We've said previously that we wouldn't accept the sunset clause and we're reiterating that now," a spokesman for Training Minister David Kemp told Reuters.
The spokesman confirmed that the bill was still regarded as a trigger for a so-called double-dissolution, a form of early election in which the Senate is dissolved with the lower house.
An election is due in early 1999 but the government can hold one in the second half of 1998 without a double-dissolution trigger.
"The Senate has inserted a sunset clause into the legislation which will ensure that this scheme operates as a trial," Democrats leader Cheryl Kernot said in a statement.

"(This is) in line with the promise made by the prime minister in his initial announcement, instead of having the capacity to be extended to all unemployed Australians at any time of the minister's choosing and to operate indefinitely without further scrutiny from the parliament."
The legislation, which is still under debate in the Senate, provides for a trial scheme in which unemployed people earn their welfare payments by working about two days a week.
The government plans to introduce the $15 million scheme later this year, pending parliamentary approval.
Debate on the bill will resume on Monday. The government needs two additional votes to pass any legislation in the non-government dominated Senate.
A Democrats spokeswoman said she expected the Senate to approve another amendment on Monday, under which the compulsory aspect of the legislation would be removed.
Both the Democrats and the Labor opposition would support this amendment, she said.
The bill is one of three items of legislation over which the government has implicitly threatened an early election.
